#### What type of PR is this?

/kind cleanup

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Some upcoming KEPs change the way effective resource requests are calculated on a pod.  

De-duplicates pod request calculation from:
- noderesources.computePodResourceRequest
- resourceAllocationScorer.calculatePodResourceRequest
- framework.calculateResource
- resources.PodRequestsAndLimitsReuse

In a few other places it eliminates an extra calculation of pod limits or requests that wasn't used.

issue_context.title: Evaluate moving Pod resources calculation to k8s.io/component-helper
issue_context.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Refactor [`computePodResourceRequest`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/108c284a330a82ce1a1f80238e4f54bf5e8b045a/pkg/scheduler/framework/plugins/noderesources/fit.go#L162:6) and [`calculateResource`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/108c284a330a82ce1a1f80238e4f54bf5e8b045a/pkg/scheduler/framework/types.go#L715) so that the shared bits can be put in k8s.io/component-helper.

### Why is this needed?

These 2 implementations have the risk of becoming out of sync. Two components depend on it: kube-scheduler and kubelet, so it qualifies for being in the component-helper repo.

I think the major complication is what to do with one of the dependencies of these calculations: [`IsScalarResourceName`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/108c284a330a82ce1a1f80238e4f54bf5e8b045a/pkg/scheduler/util/utils.go#L145), which depend on `k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/apis/core/v1/helper`. We need to evaluate if such check is actually necessary (that is, if removing it would change behavior). I have the suspicion that it wouldn't, assuming an apiserver already validated the Pod on admission.
comments: @liggitt for thoughts on whether this is a bad idea.

what are the consequences if the implementations get out of sync?
One of the functions governs the cached pods, and the other a pod being scheduled. So the risk is miscalculation of used resources, which could end up in overprovisioning or underprovisioning.

review_comments: This previously ignored the InPlacePodVerticalScaling feature gate for everything except for huge-pages.  It now considers it for all resources.  I haven't convinced myself it needs to consider it at all since I *think* this is only called prior to the pod scheduling and possibly being resized.  @vinaykul , any thoughts?

I'm not sure what is of concern, could you please provide some more context?

AFAIK, the function gathers the pod requests and limits at the time `ResourceConfigForPod` is invoked, and uses that information to decide whether to update the pod cgroup numbers before or after updating containers depending on whether the resize is a net increase or decrease respectively.

I guess the strangeness/asymmetry here is that for cpu and memory we calculated directly from PodSpec but for hugepages we consired whether InPlacePodVerticalScaling has been enabled (and take the values from pod spec or status). I don't fully understand this

Yes, that was it. Before this change `ResourceConfigForPod` got request/limits from `resource.PodRequestsAndLimits` which only pulls values from the requests of containers/init containers while hugepages considered InPlacePodVerticalScaling.
Any comments @vinaykul? I think this PR looks good to be merged except I'd like to understand this particular detail
can you please explicitly return the values here and remove the named return variables
This was previously ignored. We need/want to add this option? @vinaykul?
please revert everything in this file, deepcopies are costly.

It's a deep copy of a resource.Quantity which is pretty cheap. With this benchmark, 
```
func BenchmarkGetRequestForResource(b *testing.B) {  
   resources := v1.ResourceList{  
      v1.ResourceCPU:    resource.MustParse("1"),  
      v1.ResourceMemory: resource.MustParse("2G"),  
      v1.ResourcePods:   resource.MustParse("25"),  
   }  
   b.ResetTimer()  
   for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ {  
      _ = GetRequestForResource(v1.ResourceCPU, &resources, true)  
      _ = GetRequestForResource(v1.ResourceMemory, &resources, true)  
      _ = GetRequestForResource(v1.ResourcePods, &resources, true)  
      _ = GetRequestForResource(v1.ResourceCPU, &resources, false)  
      _ = GetRequestForResource(v1.ResourceMemory, &resources, false)  
      _ = GetRequestForResource(v1.ResourcePods, &resources, false)  
   }  
}
```

benchstat shows the updated version is slower, but its only (154-87.5)/6 =~ 11 ns slower per call so essentially negligible:
```
name                      old time/op  new time/op   delta
GetRequestForResource-12  87.5ns ± 2%  154.0ns ± 1%  +75.97%  (p=0.000 n=10+9)
```

I think retaining units in the quantity helps some, but happy to revert if you disagree.
@vinaykul Was there a reason this didn't check the if `pod.Status.Resize == v1.PodResizeStatusInfeasible` in this calculation?

Just thinking out loud: If I'm not mistaken, quota evaluation happens much earlier in the workflow. Once the pod has been accepted by a node, a subsequent resize that leads to PodResizeStatusInfeasible does not alter the pod's quota usage. The pod will still be using whatever it was admitted at by the node. I do see your point that we may be overdoing it, but we made a conscious choice to conservatively use max here and err on the side of caution. It can always be relaxed later.
